title: jq in Depth: Filter, Reshape, and Summarise JSON
intro: Every cloud CLI and API speaks JSON, and jq is how the shell reads it. Beyond picking out one field, it filters, reshapes, and counts, which replaces a lot of throwaway scripts. The file pods.json holds the output of 'kubectl get pods -A -o json'.

steps.prompt: Count the pods: the length of the items array in pods.json.
steps.why: A jq program is a pipeline: '.items' selects the array and '| length' counts it. The pipe inside the quotes is jq's own, passing each result to the next filter. Single quotes around the program stop the shell interpreting it.

steps.prompt: Print the names of the pods whose phase is not Running, as plain text.
steps.why: '.items[]' turns the array into a stream of objects, 'select' keeps those matching a condition, and the last filter picks a field. -r prints raw strings without JSON quotes, which is what you want when the output feeds another command. This one pattern, iterate, select, project, covers most everyday jq.

steps.prompt: Summarise: count the pods in each phase. Group the items by .status.phase and output an object with the phase and the count for each group.
expected_commands: jq '.items | group_by(.status.phase) | map({phase: .[0].status.phase, count: length})' pods.json
jq -c '.items | group_by(.status.phase) | map({phase: .[0].status.phase, count: length})' pods.json
steps.hint: jq '.items | group_by(.status.phase) | map({phase: .[0].status.phase, count: length})' pods.json
steps.explanation: One object per phase with its count.
steps.why: group_by makes an array of arrays, one per distinct value; map then turns each group into a small object, taking the phase from the group's first member. It's the jq form of SQL's GROUP BY, and it replaces the 'sort | uniq -c' idiom when the data is JSON.

steps.prompt: Make a tab-separated table of namespace, name, and node for every pod.
steps.fake_output:
shop	api-6c9d7f5b8-7hm2n	ip-10-0-1-21.ec2.internal
shop	cart-5f8d9c7b6-k2m4x	ip-10-0-2-88.ec2.internal
kube-system	coredns-7db6d8ff4d-9xq2l	ip-10-0-1-21.ec2.internal
...
steps.explanation: One line per pod, with fields separated by tabs.
steps.why: Build an array of the columns, then format it: @tsv for tabs, @csv for a spreadsheet. Tab-separated output goes straight into sort, cut, awk, and 'column -t', so jq handles the JSON and the classic tools handle the rest.

steps.prompt:
A deploy script reads an image tag with jq from release.json and uses it. Which flag makes jq exit non-zero when the result is null, so the script stops instead of deploying ':null'?
  a) -r
  b) -e
  c) -c
  d) -n
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
$ jq -r '.tag' release.json ; echo "exit=$?"
null
exit=0
$ jq -er '.tag' release.json ; echo "exit=$?"
null
exit=1
steps.hint: By default a missing field isn't an error in jq.
steps.explanation: -e sets the exit status from the result: non-zero for null or false.
steps.why: A missing key gives null and exit 0, and -r prints it as the text 'null', which a script will happily use as a value. That's a real outage pattern (scripting-incident-003). Use 'jq -e' wherever a value is required, together with 'set -euo pipefail' in the calling script, or give an explicit fallback with the '//' operator.

steps.prompt: Pass a shell value into jq safely. The file services.json is an array of objects with an env field. Select those whose env equals the value 'prod', passing it as a jq variable named env.
steps.why: --arg hands the value to jq as data. The alternative, breaking out of the quotes to splice a shell variable into the program text, fails on values containing quotes and lets the value be interpreted as jq code. The same rule applies everywhere: pass values as parameters, never by building program text from them.
